sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, Zhou Dynasty
sources.note: Directly read institutional overview. Used only for independent rival states, seven major kingdoms, Qin unification in 221 BCE and competing philosophies. Its broad Eastern Zhou label runs to 221; royal dynasty ending in 256 is distinguished using Met chronology.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, China, 1000 BCE to 1 CE: Chronology
sources.note: Directly read dynasty timeline: Eastern Zhou 770 to 256 BCE; Warring States 475 to 221; Qin 221 to 206; Western Han begins 206. The later prose has a conspicuous 206 BCE heading attached to Qin establishment; that typo is excluded. No claim of equivalence between ancient imperial and present borders used.

sources.title: Columbia University Asia for Educators, Book of Lord Shang: Making Orders Strict
sources.note: Directly read primary-source translation and institutional introduction. Fourth-century BCE Qin reform emphasis on agriculture, war and written rewards/punishments. A normative political program, not proof of universal obedience.

sources.title: Agricultural practices of the Qin people from the Warring States period to the Qin Dynasty: Matengkong, Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution (2022)
sources.note: Directly read research article methods, results, table 2 and Discussion. The 87 samples deliberately combine Warring States and Qin-dynasty contexts because the authors cannot separate them reliably; public copy retains that span. Seed counts are not meal proportions or yield figures.

sources.title: National Museum of China, Phoenix Homeland: Bronze Age Art of Zeng and Chu, square bronze jian-fou
sources.note: Directly read Chinese exhibition catalogue, heading 铜方鉴缶. Excavated 1978 in Marquis Yi tomb; nested wine/ice vessels, securing hooks and recovered ladle. No claim of earliest refrigerator or ordinary household access.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Food serving vessel (Dou), collection record 49141
sources.note: Directly read object record: fifth to fourth century BCE painted earthenware substitute made for burial; comparable Zhongshan tomb finds. Collection object is not falsely given the comparanda’s excavation provenance.

sources.title: University of Michigan Museum of Art, Mirror with serpentine interlaces and angular meanders, 1958/2.76
sources.note: Directly read object record and 2009 gallery label. Thin bronze, flat polished reflecting face, dragon-derived ornament on reverse; elite personal accessory.

sources.title: Hubei Provincial Museum, Introduction to Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng
sources.note: Directly read museum text, introductory dating and catalogue items 5 and 6. Burial around 433 BCE supported by dated Chu bell gift. Duck case’s female ownership is museum interpretation, not certainty. Star chest’s proposed exact observation date is omitted.

sources.title: Smithsonian Music, In Sync: Ancient Chinese Bronze Bells at the Smithsonian
sources.note: Full indexed original text read; direct request rejected. Query: site:music.si.edu "In Sync" "two" bells. Lens-shaped cross-section and different strike points explain two pitches. Avoid total-bell ambiguity: 64 double-tone bells plus gift bell, not 64 objects in entire ensemble.

sources.title: Hubei Provincial Museum, The Marquis Yi of Zeng: Lacquer Objects
sources.note: Directly read museum-authored exhibit hosted on Google Arts & Culture, instruments, rotating-head deer and lacquered shield. Museum’s inference of deer as drum stand retained as interpretation.

sources.title: Maddalena Poli and Yumeng Li, New Manuscript Evidence on the Formation of the Analects, Early China 47
sources.note: Directly read HTML, The Wangjiazui Kongzi said Manuscript section and note 62 on interpretative transcription. Excavated M798 in 2019 to 2021, c.300 BCE, approximately 800 strips total, scribal evidence and exact 孔子曰 formula. Not the unprovenanced Anhui collection. Erratum DOI 10.1017/eac.2025.10036 checked: table 1 images of 我 were reordered; sample formula unaffected.

sources.title: Andrew Meyer, Only the Human Way May Be Followed: Reading the Guodian Manuscripts against the Mozi, Early China 37 (2014)
sources.note: Directly read scholarly abstract. Guodian tomb 1 texts buried in Chu around 300 BCE. Interpretation that contradictory texts formed resources against intellectual opponents explicitly attributed to Meyer. No tomb occupant identified as a known teacher.

sources.title: Lisa Raphals, Divination and Medicine in China and Greece, East Asian Science, Technology, and Medicine 24 (2005), pages 78 to 103
sources.note: Directly read author-hosted PDF, printed pages 80 to 86. Web metadata gives an unrelated article title, but actual PDF title/header and content are Raphals. Shao Tuo, Baoshan tomb 2, dated 318 to 316 BCE divinations, illness and disagreement. Do not infer modern diagnosis or therapeutic efficacy.

sources.title: British Museum, Money Gallery large print guide, Case 1: China
sources.note: Full indexed original Case 1 text read after direct fetch failure. Knife forms and different state coin types. Shared-work reuse counted against current Carthaginian Empire and Celts runtime cards.

proposedOverrides.name: Zhou States and the Warring States
proposedOverrides.summary: Rival Zhou-era states, their communities and material achievements before Qin unification.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Distinct aggregate-state narrative, no alias association with eastern-zhou or western-zhou.
batchIdentityNotes.mapWindow: 500 to 200 BCE. Conventional 475 BCE phase boundary is not an exact beginning of all rivalry. Royal dynasty ends 256 BCE; Warring States system ends 221 BCE. Final phase openly identifies Qin and early Han overlap.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Decoded 500/400 BCE bounds [104.324,27.067,122.392,40.351]; 323/300 BCE [105.083,25.259,124.106,42.118]. One broad region cannot show shifting borders or a single sovereign state. Public overview cautions both aggregation and late imported endpoint.
batchIdentityNotes.sourceLimits: Smithsonian bells and BM money guide read as indexed original after direct rejection. Other cited sources directly read, including full HTML scholarly writing paper and its erratum. Matengkong evidence spans both Warring States and Qin contexts. Noble tomb evidence remains explicitly elite; medical beliefs do not become modern treatment advice.
